entities.name: Artaxerxes II
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Artaxerxes II Mnemon (r. 404–358 BCE) was the longest-reigning Achaemenid Great King of Persia, son of Darius II and Parysatis. His accession followed the Peloponnesian War’s end and was immediately contested by his brother Cyrus the Younger, whose rebellion—chronicled by Xenophon in the Anabasis—ended in Cyrus’s death at Cunaxa (401 BCE). Artaxerxes II thereafter managed a vast empire facing Egyptian secession, satrapal revolts, Greek mercenary entanglements, and renewed war with Greek cities, including the King’s Peace (Peace of Antalcidas, 387/386 BCE) that reasserted Persian arbitration over Greece.

Ancient Greek authors dominate the narrative, often hostile or Hellenocentric, yet Artaxerxes II’s longevity indicates effective, if embattled, imperial management. He sponsored building at Susa, Ecbatana, and Persepolis, and later tradition associates him with the cult of Anahita. His reign marks both the resilience and the structural strains of late Achaemenid rule before the fourth-century crises that preceded Alexander.
